reasons: A uses <= so touching intervals merge, uses max() so nested intervals are handled, and builds fresh lists so the input is not mutated. B fails two explicit requirements: touching intervals are not merged, and nested intervals shrink the result.

objections.claim: Strict < means touching intervals are not merged. Input [[1,2],[2,3]] returns [[1,2],[2,3]] instead of [[1,3]], violating requirement 3, which is the main purpose of the change.
The end is overwritten instead of taking the max. Input [[1,10],[2,3]] returns [[1,3]] instead of [[1,10]], which silently drops coverage. Input [[1,10],[2,3],[5,6]] is also wrong.

Sorting the raw pairs and unpacking assumes every pair has exactly 2 elements. A malformed 3-element pair raises ValueError. This is outside the stated input contract and minor. Empty input returns [] correctly and single-element input is fine.

allegations.claim: The docstring claims correct merging, but the code does not merge touching intervals and does not take the max end, so the claim is misleading.

allegations.quote:
robust, production-grade implementation of interval
merging with full type annotations and comprehensive documentation.
allegations.claim: The module docstring overstates quality given the two correctness bugs.

out_of_lane_notes: B's copy of each pair via list(pair) is fine, but A also avoids mutating the input because it appends new [start, end] lists. B adds a module docstring and typing noise that the task did not ask for.
